description: We want to change the world.
summary: What if we could assess a site before a rover arrives there? In 2005, the Opportunity rover became stuck in a Martian dune. This inspired TerraRover, a platform that compares Earth, Mars and Moon terrains using geospatial data and 3D models to support future robotic exploration. TerraRover: understanding the terrain before exploring it.
details:
TerraRover is a multidisciplinary project that connects geospatial characterization, quantitative terrain comparison, and robotic simulation. We transform digital elevation models (DEMs) into traceable terrain products, investigate similarities through numerical terrain descriptors, and reconstruct selected surfaces in Webots for controlled rover experiments.

Data → Geospatial processing → Morphological analysis → 3D terrain reconstruction → Rover experiment → Telemetry and interpretation

These are related but distinct stages. A high morphological similarity score is not proof that two locations have the same geology, and successful navigation in Webots is not proof of real-world planetary mobility.

How it works: methodology

A. Preparing scientific terrain datasets

Our geospatial workflow processes elevation products from Earth and planetary missions, including terrestrial DEM sources and Martian and lunar datasets such as MOLA and LOLA. For selected regions, we prepare 5 km × 5 km terrain products, subject to each source's original resolution and coverage.

Outputs include a numerical DEM.tif (the scientific elevation surface), a georeferenced Mapa_2D.tiff, a preview Mapa_2D.png, an interactive Terreno_3D.html, a geometric Terreno_3D.obj, and metadata/audit files. We document spatial characteristics and data provenance so the products can be interpreted and reused appropriately.

The numerical DEM and the colored map serve different purposes: calculations of elevation, slope, and ruggedness must be performed on the scientific DEM, not on a rendered RGBA map.

B. Investigating topographic similarity

We developed an exploratory Python comparison prototype using seven terrain descriptors: hypsometric integral, mean slope, slope variability, elevation skewness, 3D-to-2D surface-area ratio, normalized Terrain Ruggedness Index (TRI), and Topographic Position Index (TPI) variability. These descriptors form feature vectors that the prototype compares using cosine similarity.

This is an initial mathematical approach, not yet a validated analogue-ranking system. The prototype requires correction of its raster inputs to use numerical elevation models, together with consistent spatial scales, appropriate feature normalization, uncertainty analysis, and independent evaluation. We therefore avoid interpreting the current similarity value as proof that two sites are scientifically equivalent.

C. Reconstructing DEMs in Webots

Our custom DEM-to-Webots tools read elevation rasters, handle spatial information and invalid values, sample terrain heights, and generate Webots worlds using an ElevationGrid representation. This connects geospatial processing to a physics-based environment where a robotic vehicle can interact with a reconstructed surface.

Scale is a major engineering constraint. A 5 km terrain represented with a coarse simulation grid cannot resolve small rocks, wheel-scale obstacles, or all local slopes. We treat regional visualization and detailed mobility evaluation as different scales of analysis, rather than assuming a large terrain model preserves every physical obstacle.

D. Experimenting with a Sojourner-based rover

The robotics module uses a Sojourner-based six-wheel rover in Webots. Its controllers support manual motion, scripted demonstrations, waypoint-oriented automatic evaluation, and a ROS 2 command mode. A supervisor collects motion and stability measurements during simulation.

Reported outputs include distance traveled, mean speed, elapsed time, roll, pitch, combined chassis inclination, detected stalls, stability-threshold events, and progress toward a waypoint. Telemetry is written to CSV, with summary results in JSON and plotting utilities for graphical inspection.

The codebase also contains a ROS 2 Jazzy bridge for communication involving velocity commands and telemetry. Its presence in the repository demonstrates implementation, while complete end-to-end operational validation should be documented separately.

A key measurement distinction is that the current maximum_slope output is derived from vehicle orientation during motion; it is not an independent measurement of the DEM's local ground slope.

Why it is creative—and who it could help

TerraRover's contribution is not just another map or rover viewer. It explores a connection between two fields that are often presented separately: planetary geospatial analysis and virtual robotic experimentation. A DEM becomes both a source of terrain descriptors and an input to an experiment with measurable rover behavior.

This workflow could support students and educators working with authentic planetary data, robotics teams designing preliminary mobility experiments, and researchers screening candidate topographic analogues for more detailed study. The software-based approach may reduce the effort required for early exploration, while preserving the need for field verification and scientific validation.

Web Integration

Our vision

What if preparing for exploration on the Moon and Mars could begin with a more rigorous understanding of landscapes on Earth?

TerraRover is a step toward that goal: a reproducible, accessible bridge from open elevation data to candidate analogue analysis and controlled robotic experiments.

TerraRover — Exploring Earth to Understand Other Worlds.

Use of Artificial Intelligence

During the development of TerraRover, our team used AI tools as supporting resources in the following areas:

  • Programming Assistance: AI helped with code development, debugging, troubleshooting, and integrating components such as Webots, Docker, and the web platform.
  • Video Production: AI-assisted tools were used to support the creation and editing of our project presentation video.
  • Research Support: AI assisted in understanding technical concepts, exploring scientific methodologies, and identifying relevant documentation.
  • Documentation and Communication: AI helped organize technical documentation, improve explanations, and refine written content.
  • Design and Visualization: AI supported the development of visual concepts and presentation materials.

All core project decisions, implementation, scientific interpretations, and final deliverables were reviewed and managed by the Killa Coders team. AI was used as an assisting tool, not as a replacement for human development or scientific judgment.
